prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm interested in acquiring LabCo, a company that manufactures specialty epoxy countertops for use in laboratories. The PE client expects the overall laboratory countertop market to grow at 10% per year. The PE firm invests in a variety of construction materials but no synergies exist between LabCo and other portfolio companies. The PE firm is looking to hold the company 5 years. LabCo manufactures only epoxy countertops; other materials in the market include phenolic, laminate, and ceramic. LabCo is currently the only manufacturer of epoxy countertops. LabCo has a manufacturing facility in the US and currently sells in North America and China.
prompt.question: The PE client would like you to assess the threat of material substitutes stealing market share. Should the PE firm acquire LabCo?

clarifying_info.a: Customers are building contractors for high schools, universities, and industrial labs.

clarifying_info.q: Has the market been growing historically?
clarifying_info.a: The market has been stable for several years and is not expected to grow on its own (the 10% growth expectation is the client's forward-looking projection).

clarifying_info.q: What profit margin does LabCo require?
Has LabCo considered manufacturing in China?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. LabCo has investigated moving manufacturing operations to China and would expect a 25% decrease in labor cost. A new facility in China would cost $15M. Local shipping costs for product made in China would be $1/sq. ft.

clarifying_info.q: What discount rate should I use?
clarifying_info.a: Assume a discount rate of 10% and value as a perpetuity.

clarifying_info.q: What is the currency conversion rate?
Are the market size numbers annual?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, they are annual sales for all laboratory countertops.

exhibits.title: Lab Countertop Material Market Share
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart showing percentage market share by material (epoxy, phenolic, laminate, ceramic) for the US and China markets, with total annual market sizes noted

data.materials: Epoxy, Phenolic, Laminate, Ceramic shown as stacked segments for each market

exhibits.title: Material Attributes — Attribute Importance
exhibits.shows: Spider/radar chart comparing four materials (epoxy, phenolic, ceramic, laminate) across five attributes: chemical resistance, heat resistance, hardness, cost, and design features, with each attribute rated 0-5

exhibits.title: Customer Feedback
exhibits.shows: Two bar charts from a customer survey (n=120): (1) what customers identify as the best laboratory countertop material, and (2) at what price discount customers would choose phenolic instead of epoxy (responses bucketed as >50%, 30-50%, 10-30%, <10%)

data.chart1_question: In general, what is the best laboratory countertop material?
data.chart2_question: At what price discount would you choose to use phenolic instead of epoxy?

exhibits.title: Material Pricing
exhibits.shows: Table of per-sq-ft prices for each material in US dollars and Chinese yuan

exhibits.title: LabCo Epoxy Cost Structure
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart showing LabCo's cost and profit breakdown per sq ft for US sales and China sales, with all product manufactured at the single US facility

data.note: All epoxy is currently manufactured in the US at a single facility

framework: 1. Current market position — understand market size, share by material, and key differences between US and China
2. Customer preferences — identify which material attributes matter most and how customers perceive each material (Exhibit 2 & 3)
3. Competitive threat from substitutes — determine which material is the closest substitute and at what price discount customers would switch
4. Pricing and cost structure — compare current epoxy vs. phenolic pricing in both markets; analyze LabCo's cost structure (Exhibit 4 & 5)
5. Strategic options — evaluate China manufacturing investment as a lever to close the price gap and gain market share
6. Investment recommendation — synthesize findings: is the acquisition attractive given growth potential and risks?

questions.prompt: Based on Exhibit 1, what do you observe about LabCo's market position in the US vs. China?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that epoxy holds a strong market share position in the US but a very small share in China. The total US market (2M sq ft/year) is much larger than China (0.5M sq ft/year). The candidate should hypothesize that differences in market share may stem from pricing gaps, different customer requirements, or competitive dynamics. Candidate should note the market has been stable.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits 2 and 3, which material poses the greatest substitute threat to epoxy, and why?
questions.guidance: Epoxy scores strongly across most performance attributes (chemical resistance, heat resistance, hardness) relative to phenolic, ceramic, and laminate. Phenolic is the closest substitute — it performs nearly as well as epoxy on key technical attributes but is cheaper. Exhibit 3 confirms most customers identify epoxy as the best material, but incomplete market penetration indicates price-performance trade-offs. The candidate should conclude phenolic is the main threat.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibits 3 and 4, calculate the current price discount of phenolic vs. epoxy in the US and China, and assess whether Chinese customers are likely to switch to phenolic.
questions.guidance: Calculate the price discount of phenolic vs. epoxy in each market. Compare the discount against the survey data in Exhibit 3 to judge switching likelihood.

math.setup: Discount = (Epoxy price - Phenolic price) / Epoxy price. Compare result to Exhibit 3 survey thresholds.
steps: China (current, made in US): 120¥ / 6 = $20 USD equivalent for epoxy sold in China (includes $6 shipping). China phenolic = 70¥ / 6 ≈ $11.67. Discount = (120 - 70) / 120 = 50/120 ≈ 42% discount

From Exhibit 3: most customers would switch at >30-50% discount — the US 20% discount is insufficient to drive switching; the China 42% discount falls in the 30-50% bucket where a large share of customers would switch
math.answer: US customers face only a 20% discount on phenolic — unlikely to switch. Chinese customers face ~42% discount — very likely to switch to phenolic, explaining epoxy's low share in China.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 5, build out LabCo's full cost structure for the US and China markets (current state) and calculate the actual selling price and profit per sq ft in each market.
questions.guidance: Candidate should read dollar values off Exhibit 5 and reconstruct both scenarios. Current state: all product made in US; shipping to China is $6/sq ft vs. $1 for US. The candidate should note that high shipping cost to China inflates total cost and compresses margin or raises price, worsening the price gap vs. phenolic.

math.setup: Use Exhibit 5 cost buckets and selling prices. Made in US, Sold in US | Made in US, Sold in China.
steps: US cost structure: Materials $4 + Shipping $1 + SG&A $1 + Labor $4 + Profit $5 = $15 (matches US price)
China cost structure (made in US): Materials $4 + Shipping $6 + SG&A $1 + Labor $4 + Profit $5 = $20 → local China price = $20 × 6 = 120¥ (matches Exhibit 4)
math.answer: US selling price $15; China selling price 120¥ ($20). The $6 shipping component to China is the key cost driver inflating the price.

questions.prompt: LabCo is considering building a manufacturing facility in China for $15M. With a 25% labor cost reduction and local shipping of $1/sq ft, what would be the new China selling price? Would this close the price gap enough to retain customers, and what is the NPV of this investment?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute new cost structure for 'Made in China, Sold in China', derive new price, recalculate the phenolic discount, assess switching likelihood from Exhibit 3, then estimate incremental profit and compare to investment cost using perpetuity valuation.

math.setup: New labor = $4 × (1 - 25%) = $3. New shipping = $1. Keep materials $4, SG&A $1, profit $5. New local price = sum × 6¥.
steps: New cost (made in China, sold in China): Materials $4 + Shipping $1 + SG&A $1 + Labor $3 + Profit $5 = $14
From Exhibit 3: at only 16% discount, very few customers would switch to phenolic — epoxy becomes much more competitive in China

Current epoxy share in China ≈ 5% (read from Exhibit 1). If LabCo can capture up to 45% share (similar to phenolic's China share or a reasonable gain estimate), incremental share gain = 45% - 5% = 40%
Annual incremental volume = 40% × 0.5M sq ft = 0.2M sq ft
Investment cost = $15M → NPV of investment = $10M - $15M = -$5M → DO NOT INVEST in China facility on this basis alone
math.answer: New China price = 84¥. Phenolic discount drops to ~16%, making switching unlikely. However, NPV of the China facility = $10M vs. $15M cost — the investment destroys value. LabCo should not build the China facility.

brainstorming.prompt: What other risks could affect LabCo's competitive position, and what additional next steps should the PE firm consider before making an acquisition decision?

categories.name: Competitive risks
ideas: Phenolic manufacturers could reduce their own costs, widening the price gap further
New entrants could begin manufacturing epoxy, removing LabCo's monopoly
Chinese local manufacturers could produce phenolic or epoxy at lower cost

categories.name: Market risks
ideas: 10% annual market growth may not materialize if lab construction slows
Regulatory changes in lab materials standards could affect demand
Currency fluctuation (¥/$) could impact China pricing competitiveness

categories.name: Operational risks
ideas: Single US manufacturing facility creates concentration risk
Labor cost increases in the US could erode margins
Supply chain disruptions for raw epoxy materials

categories.name: Strategic risks
ideas: No synergies with PE firm's existing portfolio companies
5-year hold period may be insufficient to realize growth upside
LabCo's growth depends heavily on market growth, not share gains

recommendation: Proceed with the acquisition of LabCo only if the 10% annual market growth assumption is well-supported — organic US market growth (strong epoxy position, ~20% phenolic discount does not drive switching) is the primary value driver
Epoxy is relatively secure in the US market given strong material performance and customer perception; phenolic does not pose a near-term substitution threat in the US
Do NOT invest in the China manufacturing facility — NPV of $10M is below the $15M facility cost, destroying value
China represents limited upside: even with local manufacturing, incremental annual profit is only $1M/year
risks: Phenolic manufacturers could reduce their manufacturing costs, widening the price gap and causing customers to switch away from epoxy — especially in China
Market growth of 10% may not materialize, undermining the investment thesis
LabCo's single-facility model creates operational concentration risk
next_steps: Investigate phenolic cost structure to assess the threat of future price reductions by competitors
Investigate epoxy growth potential in other geographic markets beyond North America and China
Look for cost reduction opportunities in LabCo's own epoxy manufacturing process
Investigate adjacencies in other laboratory surfaces where epoxy could be applied (shelving, cabinets, desks)
Conduct further due diligence on LabCo management team and organizational structure
Investigate cross-selling opportunities with other PE portfolio companies despite stated lack of synergies
